## What went wrong

The reconciliation job had run nightly for eight months without incident. A
merchant onboarding campaign had raised the merchant count past the pool size for
the first time, so the job's connection usage crossed a threshold nobody had
written down.

Restarting the service cleared the symptom but not the cause. Had the job been
scheduled to retry, the incident would have recurred within the hour.
## Decision

Webhook deliveries are enqueued and delivered by a separate worker pool.

The queue is durable, so a delivery survives a deploy. Retries use exponential
backoff with jitter, capped at twenty-four hours, after which the delivery is
moved to a dead letter queue and the customer is notified by email.
# ADR-0004: Use a message queue for outbound webhooks

Sample material written for this repository's benchmark. Not a description of any
real system.
## Consequences

Delivery is now asynchronous, so the API can no longer report whether a webhook
arrived. Customers who relied on that behaviour must poll the deliveries endpoint
instead.

A slow customer endpoint now consumes a worker from the delivery pool rather than
from the request pool, so it degrades webhook delivery for everyone but leaves the
API unaffected. That is a better failure mode, not an absent one.
## Actions

The reconciliation job now uses a dedicated connection pool sized independently of
the request pool, which is the same separation the platform applies to agent
workloads. Pool saturation is now alerted at 80 per cent, and merchant count is
part of the capacity review.
## What went right

The alert fired on user-visible latency rather than on pool utilization, so it
described the impact rather than a proxy for it. The on-call engineer found the
correct runbook in under three minutes.
# Postmortem: INC-2451, checkout latency

Sample material written for this repository's benchmark. Not a description of any
real system.
## Context

Outbound webhooks were delivered inline, inside the request that produced the
event. A slow customer endpoint therefore held one of our request workers for its
entire timeout, and a customer whose endpoint was down could consume a meaningful
share of our capacity by doing nothing at all.

Retries were attempted in the same request, which meant a delivery either
succeeded within one request's lifetime or was lost.

cases.question: Does cordoning a node stop the pods that are already running on it?
cases.text: No, cordoning a node does not stop the pods that are already running on it. Cordoning only stops the scheduler from placing new pods on the node, but the pods already running keep running and the node continues serving traffic until those pods are moved by eviction [1].

checks.quote:
## Draining a node

Cordon the node first so the scheduler stops placing new pods on it. Cordoning is
not eviction: pods already running keep running, and the node keeps serving
traffic until they are moved.

Once the node is cordoned, evict the running pods and wait for them to reschedule
elsewhere. Eviction respects pod disruption budgets, so a workload that declares
one will be moved a replica at a time.

## Draining a node

Cordon the node first so the scheduler stops placing new pods on it. Cordoning is
not eviction: pods already running keep running, and the node keeps serving
traffic until they are moved.

Once the node is cordoned, evict the running pods and wait for them to reschedule
elsewhere. Eviction respects pod disruption budgets, so a workload that declares
one will be moved a replica at a time.
## Returning a node to service

Uncordon the node once it has rejoined the cluster and reports Ready. Do not
uncordon a node that is Ready but has not yet pulled its DaemonSet images: it will
accept pods it cannot run.
## Kernel upgrades

Nodes are drained before any kernel upgrade, without exception. An in-place kernel
upgrade on a node that is still serving traffic has caused two of our three
longest outages.

Reboot the node after the packages are installed. A kernel that is installed but
not booted reports the new version to the package manager and the old version to
the running system, which makes every subsequent audit wrong.
## Known issues

Eviction stalls indefinitely when a pod has no disruption budget and its
controller will not create a replacement — a single-replica StatefulSet is the
usual cause. Delete the pod directly after confirming the workload tolerates it.

cases.question: Why would an eviction never finish?
cases.text: An eviction would never finish if a pod has no disruption budget and its controller will not create a replacement. A common example of this situation is a single-replica StatefulSet. In such cases, eviction stalls indefinitely, and the recommended action is to delete the pod directly after confirming the workload tolerates it [1].

## Declaring an incident

Declare an incident when customer impact is confirmed or when you need more than
one person. Declaring early costs a channel and a status page entry. Declaring
late costs the timeline, because nobody was writing anything down.
## Authentication

Every request requires a bearer token. Tokens are validated against the tenant's
key set; the service stores no credentials and issues no tokens of its own.

cases.question: What caused INC-2451?
cases.text: INC-2451 was caused by connection pool exhaustion in the payments service. This exhaustion was triggered by a background reconciliation job that opened one connection per merchant and held it for the duration of its run. The merchant onboarding campaign had increased the merchant count past the pool size for the first time, causing the job's connection usage to cross a threshold that had not been documented. Restarting the service cleared the symptom but not the underlying cause, and if the job had been scheduled to retry, the incident would have recurred within the hour [2][3].

# Postmortem: INC-2451, checkout latency

Sample material written for this repository's benchmark. Not a description of any
real system.
## What went wrong

The reconciliation job had run nightly for eight months without incident. A
merchant onboarding campaign had raised the merchant count past the pool size for
the first time, so the job's connection usage crossed a threshold nobody had
written down.

Restarting the service cleared the symptom but not the cause. Had the job been
scheduled to retry, the incident would have recurred within the hour.
## Summary

Checkout p99 latency rose from 240 ms to 9 s for 47 minutes. No requests were
lost. The cause was connection pool exhaustion in the payments service, triggered
by a background reconciliation job that opened one connection per merchant and
held it for the duration of its run.
## What went right

The alert fired on user-visible latency rather than on pool utilization, so it
described the impact rather than a proxy for it. The on-call engineer found the
correct runbook in under three minutes.
## Timeline

The reconciliation job started at 02:00 UTC on its usual schedule. Latency alerts
fired at 02:14 once the pool was fully consumed. The on-call engineer restarted
the payments service at 02:41, which cleared the pool and restored latency
immediately. The job was disabled at 02:47 and the incident closed at 03:01.
## Actions

The reconciliation job now uses a dedicated connection pool sized independently of
the request pool, which is the same separation the platform applies to agent
workloads. Pool saturation is now alerted at 80 per cent, and merchant count is
part of the capacity review.
## Writing the postmortem

Every severity one and two gets a written postmortem within five working days.
Postmortems are blameless: they describe what the system allowed to happen, not
who was unlucky enough to be holding the pager.
## Kernel upgrades

Nodes are drained before any kernel upgrade, without exception. An in-place kernel
upgrade on a node that is still serving traffic has caused two of our three
longest outages.

Reboot the node after the packages are installed. A kernel that is installed but
not booted reports the new version to the package manager and the old version to
the running system, which makes every subsequent audit wrong.

cases.question: How long do I have to acknowledge a page, and what happens if I do not?
cases.text: You have to acknowledge a page within five minutes. If a page is still unacknowledged after ten minutes, it escalates to the secondary, and after twenty minutes it escalates to the engineering manager [1].

checks.quote:
## Acknowledging a page

is not a commitment to fix alone — it means someone has eyes on the alert.

and after twenty to the engineering manager.

## Severity

Severity one means the product is unusable for a substantial share of customers,
or data is at risk. Severity two means a major feature is degraded with a
workaround. Everything else is severity three and waits for business hours.

Severity is set by impact, not by cause. A database failover that nobody noticed
is not a severity one.
## Writing the postmortem

Every severity one and two gets a written postmortem within five working days.
Postmortems are blameless: they describe what the system allowed to happen, not
who was unlucky enough to be holding the pager.
## Declaring an incident

Declare an incident when customer impact is confirmed or when you need more than
one person. Declaring early costs a channel and a status page entry. Declaring
late costs the timeline, because nobody was writing anything down.
## What went wrong

The reconciliation job had run nightly for eight months without incident. A
merchant onboarding campaign had raised the merchant count past the pool size for
the first time, so the job's connection usage crossed a threshold nobody had
written down.

Restarting the service cleared the symptom but not the cause. Had the job been
scheduled to retry, the incident would have recurred within the hour.
## Summary

Checkout p99 latency rose from 240 ms to 9 s for 47 minutes. No requests were
lost. The cause was connection pool exhaustion in the payments service, triggered
by a background reconciliation job that opened one connection per merchant and
held it for the duration of its run.
## Actions

The reconciliation job now uses a dedicated connection pool sized independently of
the request pool, which is the same separation the platform applies to agent
workloads. Pool saturation is now alerted at 80 per cent, and merchant count is
part of the capacity review.
## What went right

The alert fired on user-visible latency rather than on pool utilization, so it
described the impact rather than a proxy for it. The on-call engineer found the
correct runbook in under three minutes.
## Draining a node

Cordon the node first so the scheduler stops placing new pods on it. Cordoning is
not eviction: pods already running keep running, and the node keeps serving
traffic until they are moved.

Once the node is cordoned, evict the running pods and wait for them to reschedule
elsewhere. Eviction respects pod disruption budgets, so a workload that declares
one will be moved a replica at a time.
